newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya coast quiet after attacks, police say.
newsitem.headline: Kenya coast quiet after attacks, police say.

text.p: Kenyan police on Monday reported no serious incidents overnight around Mombasa on the Indian Ocean coast, where a dozen suspects from five days of mayhem were to appear in court.

But legal sources said the fact that the 12 would be charged in Mombasa with carrying offensive traditional weapons -- such as bows and arrows -- and endangering lives showed they were not at the heart of the attacks that have killed at least 31 people.
"We are still talking to the main suspects. We are holding some," Kenya Police spokesman Peter Kimanthi said.
"As far as I know there was no violence overnight but that doesn't mean there was absolutely none and we might hear about it later," he said.
He declined to say anything more about the main suspects of the violence, which President Daniel arap Moi has blamed on opposition leaders fanning tribal hatred ahead of elections due this year.
Some opposition leaders accuse Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) of orchestrating the attacks, which police say are well-planned.

Kimanthi said 69 people had been arrested since raiders attacked police posts just south of Mombasa last Wednesday, killing six policemen and eight civilians and stealing nearly 30 rifles and ammunition.

The raid was followed by a hunt by police, the army and the navy for the well-organised attackers. But the operation failed to stop a string of new attacks on villages, a petrol station, a tourist lodge and the burning of kiosks along Diana Beach south of Mombasa.
Police blamed thugs for the killings but gave few details.
Arsonists razed about 100 roadside kiosks and set fire to dozens of houses around Mombasa on Sunday after five Kenyans were killed and many hurt overnight, witnesses said.
"We are treating this as thuggery and do not see a political motive. The situation is fluid but it is under control. It took us by surprise," said Coast police chief Francis Gichuki.

He said those detained included two members from the Safina party who were under questioning. Safina, which has not been officially registered, has campaigned for political reforms and an end to corruption.
Thousands of foreign tourists were advised to stay in their beach hotels on the coast north and south of Mombasa but officials said no visitors had been caught up in the violence.
Residents said those Kenyans killed were mainly people who originally came from outside the coastal region. They pointed to leaflets, hand-written in Swahili, which had been distributed in the area.

"The time has come for us original inhabitants of the Coast to claim what is rightly ours. We must remove these invaders from our land," said the pamphlets, which echoed ethnic slogans painted on walls and roads near some of the clash cites.
Karl-Heinz Straus, chairman of the Coastal Kenya Association of Tour Operators, said the violence could damage the tourism industry which earned about $465 million last year from 770,000 visitors.
Nairobi newspapers said on Monday hundreds of Kenyans had crowded aboard buses and trains on the coast at the weekend in an attempt to return to their birthplaces deeper inside Kenya.

The newspapers said the outbreak of conflict on the coast with presidential and parliamentary elections due this year appeared to be similar to ethnic violence in Kenya's Rift Valley before and after 1992 elections.
No date has yet been set for the polls at which Moi, aged 73 and in power for 19 years, will be seeking a new five-year term.
